passage:
By nine in the morning, Akash had been in the block office line for two hours with his scholarship papers. About forty people stood in a bent line under the tin roof. Kamal, a boy from his college, stood just behind him.
A man in a crisp white shirt walked straight to the window. The clerk stood up and said, “Sir, please come inside.” The man was ahead of them all within a minute.
“Every time,” an old man muttered. Nobody else spoke. Akash felt heat in his chest, and his hands closed tight on the papers. He took a breath and asked the clerk politely, “Is there a separate window? We have been waiting since seven.” The clerk didn’t look up.

qa.q: How long had Akash been in the block office line?
qa.a: He had been in the line for two hours with his scholarship papers.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling as his hands closed tight on the papers?
qa.a: He felt angry and helpless. The heat in his chest and the tight hands show that he was upset, but the clerk did not respond to his question.

qa.q: What small choice did Akash make instead of staying silent or exploding?
qa.a: He took a breath and asked the clerk politely whether there was a separate window. He spoke up without insulting anyone.

qa.q: How might Kamal, standing behind Akash, have taken this scene?
qa.a: Kamal may have felt the same anger but stayed quiet like the others, or may have felt encouraged that Akash spoke. The passage does not say which.

grounding: Shows a patient person watching someone with influence go to the front, and feeling anger and helplessness.

passage:
Rafael had queued for ninety minutes outside the housing office in Lisbon, his folder pressed to his chest. Oskar, an exchange student from Sweden, stood behind him, checking the time on his phone.
A man in a tailored coat strolled up to the door and shook the guard’s hand. “Good to see you again,” the guard said, and pushed the door open for him.
A woman near the front sighed loudly. A teenager looked away. Rafael’s jaw tightened. “I’ve been standing here since eight,” he said, half to himself.
Oskar leaned over. “Do you want to ask the guard together? Calmly.” Rafael nodded slowly, not sure it would help.

qa.q: Where was Rafael queuing?
qa.a: Rafael was queuing outside the housing office in Lisbon.

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling when his jaw tightened?
qa.a: He was angry and felt helpless at how easily the man skipped the line, even after ninety minutes of waiting. He nodded slowly because he doubted it would help.

qa.q: What did Oskar offer that gave Rafael a way to act?
qa.a: Oskar suggested they ask the guard together, calmly. That made objecting feel less lonely and less like a fight.

qa.q: How might the man in the tailored coat see the moment?
qa.a: He may not even realise anyone minded, since he simply greeted the guard as usual. The passage shows only what he did, so what he thinks is a guess.

grounding: Shows a patient person seeing someone with influence go to the front, feeling anger and helplessness, and a way to object calmly.

subtype: Queue jumped by a well-connected person [Receiver]
passage: At the university admissions office, Charu and her friend Ira had been in the queue since seven, clutching their files. At eleven, a man in a crisp kurta walked straight past forty students and into the registrar's room, waving a letter. 'Minister's reference,' someone whispered. The clerk stood up and smiled at him. Charu felt heat rise in her chest. Her own file had taken three trips to get right. Ira muttered, 'That's how it works here. Forget it.' Around them, most students looked at the floor. But one older student said loudly, 'Sir, is there a separate line for references?' The clerk ignored him. Charu said nothing. On the way home, though, she wrote to the university's grievance email, and felt a little less small.

qa.q: Since what time had Charu and Ira been in the queue?
qa.a: Since seven.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when the man walked past?
qa.a: Anger and helplessness, heat rising in her chest after waiting since seven and making three trips.

qa.q: What options did the students have, and which did Charu choose?
qa.a: Accept it like Ira, object aloud like the older student, or complain formally; Charu wrote to the grievance email, a calm and safe way to object.

qa.q: How does Ira seem to see the queue-jumping?
qa.a: As normal and not worth fighting, having learned to accept that 'that's how it works here'.

grounding: A student watches someone with influence skip a long queue, feels angry and helpless, and chooses a way to object.

passage:
Dear Vaibhav,
You asked why I sounded upset on the phone. We were at the government hospital for Maa's scan. We'd been waiting four hours. Then a man walked in with two assistants and a phone to his ear, and the ward attendant took him straight in. Someone said he was a big contractor. Maa squeezed my hand and said, 'Let it go, beta.' I couldn't. I was so angry my hands shook, and so helpless, because what could I do? A lady next to us, waiting with her father, said, 'This happens every time.' That's what scared me: everyone just accepted it.
In the end I asked at reception, calmly, how the order is decided. The nurse looked embarrassed and moved Maa up two places.
I'm still angry.
Shreya

qa.q: How long had Shreya and Maa been waiting?
qa.a: Four hours.

qa.q: What did Shreya feel when the man was taken straight in?
qa.a: So angry that Shreya's hands shook, and helpless, unsure what could be done.

qa.q: What did Shreya's calm question achieve?
qa.a: Asking reception how the order is decided made the unfairness visible and got Maa moved up two places.

qa.q: How might the lady waiting with her father see the situation?
qa.a: She seems resigned, saying 'This happens every time', having learned to accept the unfairness.

grounding: A young adult waiting at a hospital sees an influential man skip the queue, feels angry and helpless, and chooses to object calmly.

subtype: Queue jumped by a well-connected person [Receiver]
passage: Bhavna, you asked what happened at the exam centre. So, this is Aditi's rant. Three hundred of us in the sun, waiting for the gate to open for document checks. Then a car pulls up, and a boy walks straight to the front with a man everyone called 'the local leader's nephew'. The guard just opened the side gate for him. I felt this hot, useless anger. My father has told me my whole life, 'Don't argue with powerful people.' And for a second I thought, fine, that's the world. But the girl next to me calmly asked the guard, 'Is there a rule for this?' Others joined in. The guard got nervous and sent the boy back to the line. I didn't say anything. I'm still thinking about why.

qa.a: Three hundred.

qa.q: What did Aditi feel when the boy walked to the front?
qa.a: A hot, useless anger mixed with helplessness, and a pull to accept it because of the father's advice.

qa.q: What did the girl next to Aditi do that worked?
qa.a: She calmly asked the guard whether there was a rule, others joined in, and the guard sent the boy back to the line.

qa.q: How might the guard have felt when the students started asking?
qa.a: Nervous and caught between pressure from a powerful family and a crowd asking about fairness.

grounding: A student watches a well-connected boy skip a queue, feels angry and helpless, and sees someone else object calmly.

passage:
Monday. Hafsa had been in the scholarship verification queue at the university office since eight, token 47, clutching her family's papers. At eleven, Madhav strolled past forty people, said "Uncle called ahead" to the clerk, and was done in five minutes. Nobody said a word. Hafsa's hands shook with anger. She said nothing either.
Wednesday. Back again, because one paper needed another stamp. A man in front of her muttered, "That's how it works. Why fight?" Hafsa nodded, and hated herself for nodding.
Friday. When a woman holding a note from "the minister's office" walked to the front, Hafsa heard her own voice: "Ma'am, we've all been here since eight. Please take a token." The clerk hesitated. Two others in the queue murmured agreement. The woman sighed and went to the back.

qa.q: What token number did Hafsa have on Monday?
qa.a: Token 47.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when Madhav was served in five minutes?
qa.a: She felt angry and helpless; her hands shook, but she stayed silent like everyone else.

qa.q: What changed by Friday, and why did it work?
qa.a: Hafsa spoke up politely, stating that everyone had waited since eight, and others backed her, so the woman had to take her place in the queue.

qa.q: How might the man who said "Why fight?" see the queue?
qa.a: He seems to have learned to accept unfairness as normal, protecting himself by not expecting better.

grounding: Shows a young woman watching well-connected people skip a queue, first accepting it in anger and helplessness, then objecting.
